study.title: Psalm 77 From Anguish to the Remembrance of God's Works
study.overview: This psalm shows a deeply slaughtered believer who, instead of sinking into despair, leads his crisis to prayer and reflection. First, he describes the night of affliction: insistent cry, insomnia, inability to speak and feel that God has moved away. Then, when the questions threaten to dominate the faith, he decides to remember the old works of the Lord and meditate on his deeds. Finally, the remembrance of God's greatness in the redemption of his people, especially in the crossing of the sea, transforms lamentation into trust: the same God who led Israel continues to be a shepherd of his people.

outline.title: Clamor at the night of distress
outline.explanation: The psalmist prays with insistence, but his soul finds no comfort. He spends the night in inner tension, thinking of God, but without being able to sleep or speak. The memories of the ancient days and his song do not immediately relieve the pain; they show that he is seeking to understand his situation before God.

outline.title: The questions of faith and the decision to remember
outline.explanation: The crisis is expressed in strong questions: Did God reject forever? Is your kindness over? Did he forget to be merciful? Then the psalmist names his pain and changes his direction: instead of insisting only on the dark present, he proposes to remember the works of the Lord, meditate on them and talk about his deeds. The memory of past wonders sustains the confession that God is holy, unique and powerful to deliver his people.

outline.title: The memory of deliverance and the shepherd who guides
outline.explanation: The psalm culminates in the language of theophany: the waters, the heavens, the thunders and the lightnings respond to the action of God. The way of God passes through the sea, although his footprints remain hidden. The conclusion is pastoral: God guided his people as a flock through Moses and Aaron.

study.context: The notes presented treat the psalm as a composition attributed to Asafe, directed to the conductor and linked to Jedutum. Matthew Henry notes that psalm may reflect personal anguish or a public calamity of the people, and Adam Clarke's notes suggest that the author speaks of the person of Israelis in captivity, although this is not right in the text itself. The immediate scenario of the chapter is the prayer of an afflicted one that goes from the lamentation to the memory of divine intervention in the past.
study.theology: The theological center of the psalm is the tension between the present experience of abandonment and the historical fidelity of God. The text does not deny pain or softens questions; on the contrary, it shows that faith can speak honestly in the face of God's perceived silence. Still, the answer is not speculation, but the reverent memory: remembering the works of the Lord reorients the heart. The psalm states that God is holy, incomparable and capable of wonders. His greatness is seen both in the judgment on the waters and in the care of leading the people as a shepherd. Thus, the past of redemption serves as a guarantee that the apparent absence of God does not amount to its definitive rejection.

scholarViews.insight: The psalmist complains that God seems to have moved away, but finds hope in recalling the past acts of God, especially during the night of prayer and meditation.
The memories of God's great works in the past help the psalmist overcome the fear that the Lord has rejected his people, showing that persevering in remembrance strengthens faith.
The repetition of the cry shows the intensity of prayer; the psalm ends with the image of God leading his people as a flock through Moses and Aaron.

questions: When affliction makes it seem that God has turned away, do I take my questions to him or just feed hopelessness?
What past works of the Lord do I need to remember more carefully so as not to misinterpret the present?
Does my prayer end in visible circumstances or confidence that God keeps guiding his people?
study.practice: Separate a time of prayer in which you sincerely name your anguish before God, as the psalmist does. Then write three acts of God's faithfulness in his history or in biblical history and meditate on them until his vision of the present is corrected by this memory. If you are in crisis, pray in community, asking brothers and sisters to help you remember the holy and powerful character of God.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not allow you to define with certainty whether the psalm was born from a strictly personal pain or a public crisis of Israel. It is also not possible to safely determine, from the material provided, which specific historical event is behind the mention of the sea and the guidance of the people.
